assignment.title: Systems of Linear Inequalities Honors (M3 T2 L5)
assignment.essentialQuestion: What does the graph of a system of linear inequalities look like, and how can you describe the solution set?
assignment.instructions: Systems of linear inequalities. Every system is graphed in the graphing workspace: each boundary line, solid or dashed, each half-plane, and the overlap where the solutions are — then you test points and describe the region. For a word problem, write the constraints in the tool before you graph them. You have 3 tries on each Warm-Up, Classwork and Practice question, with hints. The Exit Ticket is one try with no hints.
assignment.teacherNotes: Algebra I Module 3 Topic 2 Lesson 5, from the district slides (three 45-minute days), TEKS A.3H with A.2H for writing the constraints. Honors version: the same lesson with standard-form systems to rewrite in the Warm-Up, Practice and Exit Ticket, a parameter (P11), a bounded region with its corners and area (P12, P13), a sort of systems by their solution sets (P14), Emma’s corners found algebraically (P15), and two audited Digital SAT items from the CCMR bank (P16, P17), so the Honors version is ready as written. Classwork order: a plain system, y > x − 2 and y ≤ −x + 4 (CW 17, added), comes first, then Activity 5.2's x + y > 1 and −x + y ≤ 3 (CW 5–6), then Noah's raft (Getting Started and Activity 5.1, CW 1–4), so students build the plain case before the word problem. Warm-Up rebuilt as readiness: one inequality graphed (Lesson 4), a point checked against two inequalities, and two constraints written for one situation. Every system is built in the Systems Workspace except Emma’s: her calorie line, 6.9x + 10.4y = 400, has no whole-number points to plot, so the tool draws her system and students test a point and choose their own (the slide says to use technology). Warm-Up and Exit Ticket are generated per student and back Recovery. Slide notes: the Getting Started "Think about…" box names Chase; the guide is Noah. On the Activity 5.4 slide the pictures of Systems B and C overlap; this file uses B: y > (3/5)x + 3 and y > −(3/5)x + 3, C: y > (3/5)x + 3 and y < −(3/5)x + 3, which match Possible Solutions B and C.

sections.title: Warm-Up — From One Inequality to Two

questions.prompt: One inequality first. Graph $y \ge {{sg|coef}}\frac{ {{pa}} }{ {{q}} }x {{b|signed}}$ and test the point (0, 0). In this lesson you graph two inequalities on one plane, and the solutions are where the shading overlaps.
directionSteps: Build the boundary line.
Choose solid or dashed.
Shade the half-plane of solutions.
Test the point.
hints: Where does the boundary cross the y-axis, and which way does the slope take you from there?
Does ≥ include the line? With y alone, does ≥ shade above or below?
Plot the y-intercept, then use the slope. ≥ includes the line, so it is solid, and it shades above; substitute (0, 0) to check.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. For ≤ or ≥, the boundary line is…

steps.title: One inequality
steps.instruction: Boundary line, then solid (≤, ≥) or dashed (<, >), then the side that makes the inequality true.

steps.title: Coming up
steps.instruction: A system graphs two inequalities on one plane. Its solutions are the points in BOTH shaded half-planes.

solutionReview.headline: Solid line, shaded above.
reasoning: Plot (0, {{b}}), then use a rise of {{p}} and a run of {{q}}.
≥ includes the line: solid. Shade above; (0, 0) checks the side.
solutionReview.commonError: Swapping the rise and the run.

questions.prompt: Two conditions at once. A point is a solution of a system only when it makes EVERY inequality true. Check both points in the system $y > x {{b1|signed}}$ and $y \le -x {{b2|signed}}$.
directionSteps: Substitute the first point into both inequalities.
Substitute the second point into both inequalities.
Decide which point solves the system.

responses.label: How many of the two inequalities does ({{p1x}}, {{p1y}}) make true?
How many of the two inequalities does ({{p2x}}, {{p2y}}) make true?
Which point is a solution of the system?

hints: What is each right side at the point’s x-coordinate? How does the point’s y-coordinate compare with it?
Substitute the x-coordinate into each right side and compare the result with the y-coordinate. A point that makes only one inequality true is not a solution of the system.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. A solution of a system must make…

steps.title: Solution of a system
steps.instruction: A point solves a system of inequalities only when it makes every inequality in the system true.

solutionReview.headline: Check each point in BOTH inequalities.
reasoning: ({{x1}}, {{yA}}): {{yA}} > {{x1}} {{b1|signed}} and {{yA}} ≤ −({{x1}}) {{b2|signed}}, so it makes both true.
({{x2}}, {{yB}}) makes y > x {{b1|signed}} true but y ≤ −x {{b2|signed}} false, so it is not a solution of the system.
solutionReview.commonError: Calling a point a solution of the system when it makes only one of the inequalities true.

questions.prompt: Two constraints, one situation. A van holds at most {{n}} people. Adults pay ${{p}} and students pay ${{q}} for a museum trip, and the trip must collect at least ${{M}}. Let x be the number of adults and y the number of students. Write an inequality for each constraint, then find what {{x0}} adults and {{y0}} students would pay.
directionSteps: Write the inequality for the seats in the van.
Write the inequality for the money.
Find the money the group would pay.

responses.label: Money paid by {{x0}} adults and {{y0}} students ($)

hints: What does each constraint count: people or dollars? Which phrase is a ceiling, and which is a floor?
Adults plus students can be at most the seats. Each group’s price times its count, added, must be at least the goal. Which symbol fits each?
"At most" is ≤ and "at least" is ≥. For the money paid, multiply each count by its price and add.

misconceptions.message: "At most" means as many people as there are seats, or fewer.
"At most" includes filling every seat.
"At least" means the trip collects the goal or more.
"At least" includes collecting exactly the goal.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. "At most" means…

solutionReview.headline: One inequality for each constraint.
reasoning: Seats: x + y ≤ {{n}}.
solutionReview.commonError: Using the same symbol for both constraints: the seats are a ceiling, the money is a floor.

questions.prompt: Graph a system of two inequalities: $y > x - 2$ and $y \le -x + 4$. Build each boundary line, choose solid or dashed for each, and shade each half-plane — the overlap is the solution set. Then test the point (0, 0), and choose a point of your own in the overlap.
directionSteps: Build both boundary lines.
Choose solid or dashed for each.
Shade each half-plane and find the overlap.
Test the marked point.
Choose a point of your own in the overlap.
hints: What are the y-intercept and the slope of each boundary line?
Which symbol leaves its line out, so that boundary is dashed? Which side does each inequality shade?
Plot each y-intercept and use each slope. y > x − 2 is dashed and shades above; y ≤ −x + 4 is solid and shades below. The solutions are where both shadings overlap.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. A point is a solution of a system when it is…
options: in at least one shaded half-plane

steps.title: Solution set of a system
steps.instruction: The solution set of a system of linear inequalities is the intersection of the solutions of its inequalities: every point in the overlap satisfies every inequality.

steps.title: Shade each one
steps.instruction: Shade each half-plane in its own way; the region shaded twice is the solution set.

solutionReview.headline: Two half-planes, one overlap.
reasoning: y > x − 2: a dashed boundary through (0, −2) and (2, 0), shaded above. y ≤ −x + 4: a solid boundary through (0, 4) and (4, 0), shaded below.
(0, 0) is in the overlap: 0 > −2 and 0 ≤ 4. The boundaries meet at (3, 1), on the dashed line, so that corner is not a solution.
solutionReview.answerSummary: above the dashed line and on or below the solid line
solutionReview.commonError: Shading only one inequality: the solution set is where both shadings overlap.

questions.prompt: Activity 5.2 — Analyzing Graphs of Systems of Linear Inequalities. Graph the system $x + y > 1$ and $-x + y \le 3$. Rewrite each inequality with y alone in the tool (notice the symbols), build both boundaries and shade. Then test the point (−8, 2), choose a point of your own, classify the solution region and find its corner.
directionSteps: Rewrite each inequality with y alone.
Build both boundary lines.
Choose solid or dashed for each.
Shade each half-plane and find the overlap.
Test the marked point and a point of your own.
Classify the region and find its corner.
hints: What do you add or subtract on each side to get y alone in each inequality?
Subtract x from both sides of the first and add x to both sides of the second. Which boundary is dashed, and which is solid?
x + y > 1 becomes y > −x + 1, and −x + y ≤ 3 becomes y ≤ x + 3. The corner is where the lines meet: is it on the dashed line?

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. For x + y > 1, the boundary is…

solutionReview.headline: Rewrite, build, shade, reason.
reasoning: y > −x + 1 (dashed, above) and y ≤ x + 3 (solid, below).
(−8, 2) satisfies neither inequality. The region is unbounded, and its corner (−1, 2) is on the dashed line, so it is not a solution.
solutionReview.commonError: Including the corner (−1, 2): it fails x + y > 1, because 1 is not greater than 1.

questions.prompt: Use the system x + y > 1 and −x + y ≤ 3. The two boundary lines cut the plane into four regions, and each point below lies in a different one: decide which inequalities it makes true. Then evaluate Ava’s claim: "The intersection point is always a solution to a system of inequalities because that is where the two lines meet."
directionSteps: Substitute each point into both inequalities.
Decide which inequalities each point makes true.
Check the point where the two boundary lines meet.
Explain why Ava is wrong.

options: both inequalities — it is in the overlap
responses.answer: both inequalities — it is in the overlap

options: both inequalities — it is in the overlap
both inequalities — it is in the overlap
both inequalities — it is in the overlap

responses.label: Why is Ava wrong?
options: At (−1, 2), x + y is not greater than 1: the point is on the dashed boundary, so it is not a solution
Ava is right: (−1, 2) is on both boundary lines, and a point on a boundary always makes its inequality true
At (−1, 2), −x + y is not at most 3: the point is on the solid boundary, so it is not a solution
An intersection point is never a solution of a system, because it sits on both boundary lines
responses.answer: At (−1, 2), x + y is not greater than 1: the point is on the dashed boundary, so it is not a solution

hints: At each point, what are x + y and −x + y? How does each compare with its right side?
A point is in the overlap only when it makes both inequalities true. At the intersection, is x + y greater than its right side, or equal to it?
Substitute each point into both inequalities. At the intersection, x + y equals its right side, and on a dashed boundary the inequality is false.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Is 1 > 1 true?

solutionReview.headline: Each region, then the corner.
reasoning: (2, 2): 4 > 1 and 0 ≤ 3, both. (0, 5): 5 > 1 but 5 ≤ 3 is false. (0, −2): −2 > 1 is false, −2 ≤ 3 true. (−8, 2): neither.
(−1, 2): x + y = 1, and 1 > 1 is false, so the intersection point is not a solution, even though both lines pass through it.
solutionReview.answerSummary: both; only the first; only the second; neither; Ava is wrong
solutionReview.commonError: Treating the intersection as a solution because the lines meet there: check it in every inequality.

questions.prompt: Getting Started — A River Runs Through It. Noah guides groups of adults and children down a river. His raft holds 800 pounds; more weight can make it sink, hit more rocks or maneuver more slowly. Each adult weighs about 200 pounds and each child about 100 pounds. Noah charges adults $75 and children $50, and his goal is to earn at least $150 each trip. Let x be the number of adults and y the number of children. Write an inequality for the most weight the raft can carry and one for the money Noah wants to collect. Together they make a system of linear inequalities that models Noah’s trips.
directionSteps: Write the inequality for the weight.
Write the inequality for the money.
Explain why both inequalities use x and y the same way.

responses.label: Why must x and y mean the same thing in both inequalities?
options: A solution must meet both constraints at once, so x and y must count the same people in each
Each inequality is about a different trip, so x and y can count different people in each of them
Only the weight inequality needs x and y, because the money depends on the prices alone
The money inequality should use other letters, because it counts dollars, not people
responses.answer: A solution must meet both constraints at once, so x and y must count the same people in each

hints: How much do x adults weigh in all? And y children? How much do they pay in all?
The total weight can be at most the raft’s limit, and the total money must be at least Noah’s goal. Which symbol fits each?
Weight: (pounds per adult)(adults) + (pounds per child)(children) ≤ the raft’s limit. Money: (price per adult)(adults) + (price per child)(children) ≥ Noah’s goal.

misconceptions.message: The raft holds at most 800 pounds: the weight can be 800 pounds or less.
Exactly 800 pounds is allowed: the raft holds that much.
Noah wants at least $150: the money can be $150 or more.
Exactly $150 meets Noah’s goal.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. The weight of x adults at about 200 pounds each is…

steps.title: Constraints
steps.instruction: In a system of linear inequalities, the inequalities are called constraints: they "constrain" the solutions to one region of the graph.

steps.title: Same variables
steps.instruction: Every inequality in a system uses the same variables, defined the same way.

solutionReview.headline: One inequality per constraint, with the same variables.
reasoning: Weight: 200x + 100y ≤ 800 (at most the raft’s 800 pounds).
Money: 75x + 50y ≥ 150 (at least Noah’s goal).
The system is both together: a trip must meet both.
solutionReview.commonError: Reversing a symbol: the raft’s limit is a ceiling (≤), the money goal is a floor (≥).

questions.prompt: Activity 5.1 — Determining Solutions to Systems of Linear Inequalities. Noah’s system is 200x + 100y ≤ 800 (weight) and 75x + 50y ≥ 150 (money). Decide whether each trip is a solution of the system, and what that means. First trip: 2 adults and 2 children. Second trip: 5 adults.
directionSteps: Find the weight and the money for the first trip.
Decide whether the first trip is a solution.
Do the same for the second trip.
Explain what the results mean for Noah.

responses.label: Is the first trip a solution of the system?
options: No — it fails only the first constraint
No — it fails only the second constraint

responses.label: Is the second trip a solution of the system?
options: No — it fails only the first constraint
No — it fails only the second constraint
responses.answer: No — it fails only the first constraint

responses.label: What do the results mean for Noah?
options: The first trip is safe and meets his goal; the second earns enough but is too heavy for the raft
The first trip is safe and meets his goal; the second is safe too, because it earns even more
The first trip is too heavy for the raft; the second is safe and earns more than enough
The first trip is safe but misses his goal; the second earns enough but is too heavy for the raft
responses.answer: The first trip is safe and meets his goal; the second earns enough but is too heavy for the raft

hints: How much do 2 adults and 2 children weigh in all? How much do they pay?
Multiply each count by its weight, and by its price, and add. Is each trip within the raft’s limit, and does it reach Noah’s goal?
A trip solves the system only when it meets every constraint: the weight at most the raft’s limit, and the money at least Noah’s goal.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. A combination is a solution of a system when it meets…

solutionReview.headline: Substitute each trip into both constraints.
reasoning: Second trip: 200(5) = 1000, more than 800, though 75(5) = 375 ≥ 150 — not a solution: the raft is overloaded.
solutionReview.answerSummary: first trip: yes; second trip: no (too heavy)
solutionReview.commonError: Calling the second trip a solution because it earns more: it must also meet the weight limit.

questions.prompt: Graph Noah’s system. Noah guides groups of adults and children down a river. His raft holds 800 pounds; more weight can make it sink, hit more rocks or maneuver more slowly. Each adult weighs about 200 pounds and each child about 100 pounds. Noah charges adults $75 and children $50, and his goal is to earn at least $150 each trip. Let x be the number of adults and y the number of children. Enter both constraints of the model in the tool, then build each boundary line, choose solid or dashed, and shade each half-plane — the overlap is the solution set. Test the marked point (2, 2), then choose a point of your own in the overlap.
directionSteps: Enter both constraints.
Build each boundary line.
Choose solid or dashed for each.
Shade each half-plane and find the overlap.
Test the marked point.
Choose a point of your own in the overlap.
hints: Where does each boundary line cross the axes? Find y when x = 0, and x when y = 0.
Can the raft carry exactly 800 pounds? Does exactly $150 meet Noah’s goal? So is each boundary solid or dashed?
Both constraints include their boundary (≤ and ≥), so both lines are solid. The solutions are the points shaded by BOTH inequalities.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. The solution set of a system is…

solutionReview.headline: Two constraints, one overlap.
reasoning: Weight: solid boundary through (4, 0) and (0, 8), shaded below. Money: solid boundary through (2, 0) and (0, 3), shaded above.
The overlap lies between the two lines; (2, 2) is in it: 600 ≤ 800 and 250 ≥ 150.
solutionReview.answerSummary: the region between the two solid lines
solutionReview.commonError: Shading only one inequality: the solution set is where both are shaded.

questions.prompt: Analyze Noah’s graph. The two boundary lines, 200x + 100y = 800 and 75x + 50y = 150, intersect at (10, −12), outside the first quadrant. Is the intersection point a solution? Describe the possible number of solutions of a system, and find a combination of rafters that is not a solution.
directionSteps: Substitute the intersection point into both expressions.
Decide whether it is a solution, and whether it makes sense for Noah.
Describe how many solutions a system can have.
Find the combination that is not a solution.

responses.label: Is (10, −12) a solution of the system?
options: Yes — it makes both inequalities true, because each one includes its boundary
No — the lines only cross there, and a crossing point is never a solution
Yes — every intersection point is a solution of every system of two inequalities
No — it makes the weight inequality false, because 800 is not less than 800
responses.answer: Yes — it makes both inequalities true, because each one includes its boundary

responses.label: Does (10, −12) make sense for Noah?
options: No — there cannot be −12 children: only whole numbers, 0 or more, make sense
Yes — it is a solution of the system, so it is a trip Noah can take with his raft
No — 10 adults would weigh 2,000 pounds, more than the raft holds
Yes — the raft holds exactly its 800-pound limit, so the trip is safe
responses.answer: No — there cannot be −12 children: only whole numbers, 0 or more, make sense

responses.label: How many solutions can a system of two linear inequalities have?
Which combination is NOT a solution for Noah?

hints: What are 200x + 100y and 75x + 50y at (10, −12)? How do they compare with the raft’s limit and Noah’s goal?
Is each boundary solid or dashed, and does it include its points? Can a trip have a negative number of children?
A solid boundary (≤ or ≥) includes its points. Check each combination of rafters in both constraints: the weight limit and the money goal.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. A point on a solid boundary line makes that inequality…

solutionReview.headline: On both solid lines: a solution, but not a sensible one.
reasoning: 200(10) + 100(−12) = 800 ≤ 800 and 75(10) + 50(−12) = 150 ≥ 150, so (10, −12) solves the system — but −12 children is impossible.
Two inequalities either share no points or share a whole region, so a system has no solution or infinitely many.
3 adults and 3 children weigh 900 pounds, more than 800.
solutionReview.answerSummary: yes, but not for Noah; none or infinitely many; 3 adults and 3 children
solutionReview.commonError: Assuming an intersection point is never a solution: it is when both boundaries are solid.

questions.prompt: Solve the system by graphing: $y > 5x + 3$ and $y < 5x - 3$. Build both boundaries and shade, then classify the solution region.
directionSteps: Build both boundary lines.
Choose solid or dashed for each.
Shade each half-plane.
Classify the solution region.
hints: How do the slopes of the two boundaries compare? What does that tell you about the lines?
Which line is higher? Does each inequality shade above or below its line?
Both lines have slope 5, so they are parallel. One inequality shades above the higher line and the other below the lower line: do the shadings ever overlap?

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Two boundary lines with the same slope are…

solutionReview.headline: Parallel boundaries, shading away from each other.
reasoning: Both lines have slope 5: they are parallel, 6 units apart on the y-axis.
The shading is above the upper line and below the lower line, so nothing is shaded twice: no solution.
solutionReview.commonError: Assuming every system has solutions: parallel boundaries can shade away from each other.

questions.prompt: Solve the system by graphing: $x \ge -5$ and $x \ge 1$. Then classify the solution region and choose a point of your own that is a solution.
directionSteps: Build both vertical boundary lines.
Choose solid or dashed for each.
Shade each half-plane.
Classify the region and choose a solution of your own.
hints: What kind of line is x = −5? And x = 1?
Does x ≥ c shade to the left or to the right of its line? Which shading lies inside the other?
Both boundaries are vertical lines: use the vertical-line method. x ≥ c shades to the right, so every point with x ≥ 1 also has x ≥ −5.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. The graph of x ≥ 1 is the half-plane…

solutionReview.headline: One half-plane inside the other.
reasoning: Both boundaries are solid vertical lines; both shade to the right.
Every point with x ≥ 1 also has x ≥ −5, so the solution set is x ≥ 1: an unbounded region.
solutionReview.commonError: Shading between the lines: both inequalities shade to the right.

questions.prompt: Activity 5.3 — Applying Systems of Linear Inequalities. Emma and her friends use the fitness room after school, where a sign gives the calories burned per minute. Emma uses the stair stepper. She has at most 45 minutes to exercise and wants to burn at least 400 calories. Let x be her minutes at light effort and y her minutes at vigorous effort. Write the system that models Emma’s workout.
directionSteps: Find the stair stepper rows of the table.
Write the inequality for the minutes.
Write the inequality for the calories.

responses.label: Calories burned in 45 minutes, all at vigorous effort

hints: Which rows of the table are about the stair stepper? What does each constraint count: minutes or calories?
Light minutes plus vigorous minutes can be at most her time. Calories per minute times minutes, for each effort, added, must be at least her goal.
Use the stair stepper rows, 6.9 for light and 10.4 for vigorous. "At most" is ≤ and "at least" is ≥; for 45 minutes at vigorous effort, multiply 45 by 10.4.

misconceptions.message: She has at most 45 minutes: her time can be 45 minutes or less.
Exercising for exactly 45 minutes is allowed.
She wants at least 400 calories: 400 or more.
Burning exactly 400 calories meets her goal.
Emma uses the stair stepper: use its two rows of the table.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Calories burned in y minutes at 10.4 calories per minute are…

solutionReview.headline: Time is a ceiling, calories a floor.
reasoning: Minutes: x + y ≤ 45.
Calories: 6.9x + 10.4y ≥ 400 (stair stepper rows).
All vigorous: 10.4(45) = 468 calories.
solutionReview.commonError: Using the treadmill or bike rates: Emma uses the stair stepper.

questions.prompt: Emma’s system is graphed for you in the tool, the way technology would graph it: x + y ≤ 45 (minutes) and 6.9x + 10.4y ≥ 400 (calories), where x is minutes at light effort and y is minutes at vigorous effort. Show where the shaded regions overlap, decide whether the marked point — 10 minutes light and 30 minutes vigorous — is a solution, then choose a solution of your own.
directionSteps: Show where the two shaded regions overlap.
Check the marked point in both inequalities.
Choose a point of your own in the overlap and check it.
hints: Does the marked point make x + y ≤ 45 true? Does it make 6.9x + 10.4y ≥ 400 true?
A point solves the system only if it makes both inequalities true. Which line does the overlap lie below, and which above?
Substitute (10, 30) into both inequalities. The overlap is below the time line and above the calorie line: choose a point there and check it in both.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Emma’s calories for x minutes light and y minutes vigorous are…

solutionReview.headline: Check the point in both inequalities.
reasoning: (10, 30): 10 + 30 = 40 ≤ 45 is true, but 6.9(10) + 10.4(30) = 69 + 312 = 381, which is less than 400 — not a solution.
A solution is below the time line and above the calorie line, for example (5, 38): 43 ≤ 45 and 34.5 + 395.2 = 429.7 ≥ 400.
solutionReview.answerSummary: not a solution; any point in the overlap
solutionReview.commonError: Checking only the time: (10, 30) fits in 45 minutes but burns too few calories.

questions.prompt: Algebraically prove whether each workout satisfies Emma’s system, x + y ≤ 45 (minutes) and 6.9x + 10.4y ≥ 400 (calories). Workout 1: 10 minutes light and 35 minutes vigorous. Workout 2: 20 minutes light and 25 minutes vigorous. Workout 3: 30 minutes light and 20 minutes vigorous.
directionSteps: Find the calories for each workout.
Check the minutes for each workout.
Decide whether each workout solves the system.
Interpret a solution.

responses.label: Workout 1
options: No — it fails only the first constraint
No — it fails only the second constraint

responses.label: Workout 2
options: No — it fails only the first constraint
No — it fails only the second constraint
responses.answer: No — it fails only the second constraint

responses.label: Workout 3
options: No — it fails only the first constraint
No — it fails only the second constraint
responses.answer: No — it fails only the first constraint

responses.label: What does the solution (10, 35) mean?
options: Emma can do 10 minutes light and 35 minutes vigorous, 45 minutes in all, and burn more than 400 calories
Emma burns 10 calories at light effort and 35 at vigorous effort, 45 calories in all
Emma can do 10 minutes light and 35 minutes vigorous, but that is more than her 45 minutes
Emma can do 10 minutes light and 35 minutes vigorous, 45 minutes in all, and burn fewer than 400 calories
responses.answer: Emma can do 10 minutes light and 35 minutes vigorous, 45 minutes in all, and burn more than 400 calories

hints: For each workout, how many calories does 6.9x + 10.4y give? How many minutes is it in all?
Substitute the light minutes for x and the vigorous minutes for y. Is the total time at most 45 minutes? Are the calories at least 400?
Calories: 6.9 times the light minutes plus 10.4 times the vigorous minutes. A workout solves the system only if it meets both constraints.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. The first constraint, x + y ≤ 45, is about…

solutionReview.headline: Substitute each workout into both inequalities.
reasoning: Workout 1: 45 ≤ 45 and 69 + 364 = 433 ≥ 400 — a solution.
Workout 2: 45 ≤ 45, but 138 + 260 = 398 < 400 — not enough calories.
Workout 3: 207 + 208 = 415 ≥ 400, but 50 minutes is more than 45 — not enough time.
solutionReview.commonError: Rounding 398 up to 400: a workout must burn at least 400 calories.

questions.prompt: Activity 5.4 — Identifying Systems of Linear Inequalities. The four systems use the same two dashed boundary lines, the rising line y = (3/5)x + 3 and the falling line y = −(3/5)x + 3, which cross at (0, 3). System A: y < (3/5)x + 3 and y > −(3/5)x + 3. System B: y > (3/5)x + 3 and y > −(3/5)x + 3. System C: y > (3/5)x + 3 and y < −(3/5)x + 3. System D: y < (3/5)x + 3 and y < −(3/5)x + 3. Graphs A, B and C each shade the solutions of one system, and Graph D is blank. Match each system to its graph, check a point, and evaluate Isabella’s claim.
directionSteps: Use each system’s symbols to decide above or below each line.
Match each system to its graph.
Check the given point against both lines.
Explain why Isabella is wrong.

responses.label: At x = 4, the rising line’s y-value, (3/5)(4) + 3, is
At x = 4, the falling line’s y-value is
So the point (4, −4) is…
options: below both lines: a solution of System D
between the lines: a solution of System A
above both lines: a solution of System B
responses.answer: below both lines: a solution of System D

responses.label: Isabella says: "Since the equations in each system are the same, the graphs and solutions should all be identical." Why is she wrong?

questions.prompt: Graph the system $ {{a|coef}}x + y \ge {{c}} $ and $ x - y > {{d}} $. Rewrite each inequality with y alone in the tool first. Then test the point (0, 0).
directionSteps: Rewrite each inequality with y alone.
Build both boundary lines.
Choose solid or dashed for each.
Shade each half-plane and find the overlap.
Test the point.

solutionReview.headline: Rewrite, build, shade.
reasoning: {{a|coef}}x + y ≥ {{c}} becomes y ≥ −{{a|coef}}x {{c|signed}} (solid, above); x − y > {{d}} becomes y < x {{nd|signed}} (dashed, below; dividing by −1 reverses the symbol).
The solution set is the region shaded by both.
solutionReview.commonError: Keeping > after dividing x − y > {{d}} by −1.

solutionReview.headline: Rewrite, then compare the parallel boundaries.
reasoning: {{m|coef}}x − y > {{c1}} becomes y < {{m|coef}}x {{nc1|signed}} (dividing by −1 reverses the symbol).
The system shades below y = {{m|coef}}x {{nc1|signed}} and above y = {{m|coef}}x {{b2|signed}}: a strip if the second line is lower, no solution if it is higher.

misconceptions.message: "At most" means the club makes that many prints or fewer.
"At most" includes making exactly that many prints.
"At most" means the supplies cost the budget or less.
"At most" includes spending exactly the budget.

solutionReview.headline: Each constraint gives a limit; the smaller limit wins.
reasoning: With x = {{x0}}: the count allows y ≤ {{cnt}}; the budget allows {{q}}y ≤ {{bud}}, so y ≤ {{bf}} whole prints.
Both must hold, so the greatest is {{G}}.
